summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward LGBT people has hardened into documented state policy. The Kaos GL report "A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy" records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, with detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants identified as the main reasons. The same report documents 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and six violations of the right to life, three of them recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would amend Civil Code Article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing interventions deemed illegal would face fines and up to seven years' prison, trans people receiving such care up to three years, and courts would be able to order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns that it would push treatment into unregulated underground settings. The draft had not been reported as enacted, and its pending status has not stopped authorities from acting on its logic.

Document checks are the routine point of contact between a trans visitor and the security forces. On 31 July 2025 police in the entertainment district of Istanbul carried out a mass roundup of trans women, recording their names and filming them without giving any official reason. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identity at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any stop therefore becomes an occasion on which a passport is read against presentation, which is a direct outing risk for a visitor whose appearance does not match the gender marker.

İzmir's own record cuts against its reputation as the country's most secular city. The 13th Pride Week and its events were banned, and in May and June 2025 police broke up Pride-related public events with batons, tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets. A visible trans community operates here, but visibility has attracted the same coercive response documented in Istanbul, and Pride organisation itself is treated as a target for prohibition rather than a protected assembly.
tangentialFactors:
İzmir is widely regarded as the most secular and LGBT-tolerant city in Turkey, which makes its 2025 record a useful floor rather than a ceiling for expectation elsewhere. Pride week was banned at the 13th edition and the dispersal involved anti-riot weaponry, so relative social tolerance did not translate into legal protection or police restraint.

The enforcement pattern runs ahead of the statute. Rights monitors and the trans women stopped in Istanbul both noted that no new law had been enacted, while identity roundups, GBT background checks and event bans were already being applied; legal experts cited in the Istanbul reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. A visitor should therefore judge risk from enforcement practice rather than from the text of the penal code.

The national numbers give scale to the local picture: 313 liberty violations in 2025 against roughly two and a half times fewer the previous year, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, six right-to-life violations of which three were classified as hate killings, and mass detentions tied to Pride participation. Istanbul supplies the clearest documented instance of identity-document roundups of trans women, but Kaos GL's totals are national and include events and detentions outside Istanbul.

Adjacent pressures shape the same space. The government's stated justification for the draft package is the protection of "the family" and "public morals", framing that Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma, and monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that officials' discriminatory rhetoric was deepening homophobia and transphobia.
localsOnly:
Residents face a documented squeeze on association and advocacy. The closure of an LGBTI+ association and the opening of criminal cases against 11 of its members for human rights work mark a change in what domestic groups can openly do, and complaints mechanisms inside state custody are reported as ineffective and capable of attracting further violence.

Trans Syrians living in İzmir were found by Mülteci-Der to be unable to find work, to face exploitation and harassment when they do find it, and to have no faith in justice. Employment and redress, not only policing, define the practical position of trans residents here.

Transition-related care is tightening at administrative level. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records.

Prison conditions for trans detainees follow registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025, and the case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison, with custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported delayed medical response, prosecutors entering two days later, and witness statements not taken.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 11th Judicial Package remains a leaked draft as reported on 29 October 2025. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not established by the sources cited here, and enforcement described in this dossier precedes any enactment.

The Kaos GL totals are national. The sources available do not break 2025 violations down by province, so the share attributable to İzmir is unresolved.

The mass identity-document roundup of trans women is sourced to Istanbul on 31 July 2025. Comparable roundups in İzmir are plausible but not documented in this inventory.

Whether the ban on İzmir's 13th Pride Week is a standing order for future editions, or specific to that year, is not stated in the sources.
